trecho: The second mission flown into Erick measured a minimum central pressure of 952 mb at 2324 UTC 18 June. The decrease in pressure occurred during a period of rapid intensification, with the minimum central pressure of Hurricane Erick dropping 24 mb in 8 hours. The intensity at landfall was estimated to be 110 kt, based in part on the deterioration in the cyclone’s satellite appearance (Fig. 7), which showed a degrading microwave structure during the three hours prior to landfall. An independent subjective Dvorak analysis using the embedded center technique yielded a data T-number of 4.5 within 30 minutes of the estimated time of landfall. However, due to Dvorak constraints, the final T-number was T5.0 with the Dvorak Current Intensity (CI) number of T6.0 or 115 kt. Objective intensity estimates from UW-CIMSS ranged from 98 to 127 kt around the time of landfall. Using a blend of these data yields the estimated 110 kt landfall intensity. The minimum central pressure at landfall was estimated to be 954 mb, based on the Knaff-Zehr-Courtney pressure–wind relationship. There were no wind observations available near the hurricane’s landfall point, which occurred along a sparsely populated section of the Mexican coastline.

trecho: According to media and government reports, Erick was responsible for at least 2 fatalities in Mexico. Of these, one was a direct fatality: a one-year-old boy drowned in a swollen river in Guerrero. The indirect fatality occurred in Oaxaca, where a man was electrocuted while assisting with post-storm debris removal. Heavy rainfall and strong winds caused widespread infrastructure damage in the Mexican states of Oaxaca and Guerrero, affecting at least 22 municipalities. Damage assessments indicated impacts to 42,552 homes, 468 schools, 1,665 km of federal highways, 1,243 km of state roads, 8 bridges, and 1 tunnel. Power outages disrupted service to at least 276,885 customers across the two states. In the town of San Jose Estancia Grande, Oaxaca, Mexico, near where the eastern eyewall moved through, wind damage was reported. Most homes and buildings in the town experienced significant roof damage, with many completely torn off. There was also significant infrastructure damage, with a large communications tower toppled, wreckage littered the town, and roads were blocked by fallen trees and power lines. The core of the most destructive damage occurred over a relatively narrow corridor, as damage was reported to have decreased dramatically near the towns of Macuernas and Pinotepa Nacional, approximately 11 n mi from where the center of Hurricane Erick made its closest approach. Agricultural losses were severe.

trecho: The genesis of Erick was well anticipated. The tropical wave from which Erick developed was first highlighted in the Tropical Weather Outlook (TWO) 138 h prior to formation (Table 3). The 7-day genesis probability was raised to the medium category nearly 60 h before formation and to the high category 30 h in advance. Two-day genesis forecasts were less skillful; low probabilities were introduced 60 h prior to formation, medium probabilities 30 h prior, and high probabilities only 18 h before development occurred. Forecasts of Erick’s genesis location were highly accurate, with the system forming within the center of each hatched-area genesis forecast, resulting in a 100% hit rate within the areas depicted in NHC’s Graphical TWO (Fig. 17). Given the system’s proximity to the southern coast of Mexico and the potential for tropical-storm-or hurricane-force winds to affect the region within 72 h, advisories were initiated on Potential Tropical Cyclone Five-E at 2100 UTC 16 June. A verification of NHC official track forecasts for Erick is presented in Table 4a. Official track forecast errors were lower than the 5-year mean at all forecast intervals. A homogeneous comparison of the official track errors with selected guidance models is given in Table 4b. The official track forecasts outperformed nearly all guidance at all forecast intervals.

trecho: After Flossie formed, it moved west-northwestward to northwestward parallel to the southwestern coast of Mexico. The storm moved over warm ocean waters of 30°C and within a low wind shear environment favorable for strengthening, Flossie rapidly intensified from a 35-kt tropical storm at 0000 UTC 30 June to a 65-kt hurricane at 0000 UTC 1 July, becoming the third hurricane of the 2025 eastern Pacific basin hurricane season. The hurricane made its closest approach to the west-central coast of Mexico as it continued to intensify on 1 July, with far outer rain bands impacting coastal areas. However, sustained tropical-storm-force winds remained offshore. Flossie began moving farther away from Mexico late on 1 July toward a weakness in the subtropical ridge caused by a mid-to upper-level trough over California, and it reached its peak intensity of 105 kt at 0300 UTC 2 July.

trecho: Genesis The possibility of Flossie’s genesis was noted more than a week in advance, but the system took longer to develop than expected. Table 2 provides the number of hours in advance of formation with the first NHC Tropical Weather Outlook (TWO) forecast in each category. A low (<40%) chance of genesis during the next 7 days was first indicated in the TWO about ten days (234 hours) before Flossie formed, and the chances were raised to the medium (40–60%) category 204 h before formation. For the 2-day forecast period, the disturbance was given a low and medium chance of genesis 168 and 102 hours before formation, respectively. The 7-day and 2-day probabilities were raised to the high categories 186 h and 24 h before formation, respectively. Despite the lack of confidence on when Flossie would form, the forecasts for the cyclone’s genesis location were very accurate and had a 100 percent hit rate, lying within every genesis area depicted in NHC’s Graphical TWO (Fig. 4). When the system had a low and medium chance of development, the location of genesis occurred on the northwestern edge of the NHC genesis area, indicating the system formed later than originally anticipated.

trecho: The genesis of Lorena can be traced back to a convectively active tropical wave that emerged off the coast of west Africa on 18 August. The wave continued to produce a large area of disorganized showers and thunderstorms during the next several days while it traveled quickly across the eastern and central tropical Atlantic. The tropical wave came close to becoming a tropical cyclone in the central tropical Atlantic before weakening as it moved across the Windward Islands late on 24 August. Convection became more intermittent as the wave traveled through the Caribbean Sea over the next few days, then became more robust as it crossed Central America beginning late on 26 August. The wave emerged over the eastern Pacific Ocean on 28 August, and convection gradually became better organized during the next several days while the system moved west-northwestward well to the south of Guatemala and southern Mexico. The thunderstorm activity became sufficiently organized by 0000 UTC 2 September for the system to be designated a tropical depression when it was located about 120 n mi south of Manzanillo, Mexico, and it became a tropical storm 6 h later. The “best track” chart of Lorena’s path is given in Fig. 1, with the wind and pressure histories shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively.

During the next couple of days, Lorena tracked northwestward over very warm waters near 30ºC, within a moist mid-level environment, while influenced by light vertical wind shear. Steady-to-rapid intensification ensued, with the cyclone becoming a category 1 hurricane (on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale) 24 h after becoming a tropical storm at 0600 UTC 3 September about 85 n mi southwest of Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. The cyclone remained a hurricane for about a day and reached its estimated peak intensity of 75 kt from 1800 UTC 3 September–0000 UTC 4 September. The evolution of a well-defined eyewall feature was captured by radar imagery from Los Cabos, Mexico, on 3 September as shown in Fig. 4. Environmental conditions became hostile rather abruptly on 4 September, as Lorena became influenced by increasingly strong southwesterly vertical wind shear while moving over progressively cooler waters below 26°C. These conditions resulted in rapid weakening of the cyclone, with Lorena losing deep convection shortly after 1800 UTC 4 September and becoming a post-tropical cyclone by 0000 UTC 5 September.

Observations also include flight-level and dropwindsonde observations from two flights of the 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron of the U.S. Air Force Reserve Command (AFRES) (Fig. 5). Data and imagery from NOAA polar-orbiting satellites including the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit (AMSU), the NASA Global Precipitation Mission (GPM), the European Space Agency’s Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT), the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites, and the Time-Resolved Observations of Precipitation structure and storm Intensity with a Constellation of Smallsats (TROPICS) satellites, among others, were also useful in constructing the best track of Lorena. The container ship OOCL Egypt (call sign VRLZ3) reported a sustained tropical-storm-force wind of 37 kt in association with Lorena at 1200 UTC 2 September while located about 85 n mi west of Manzanillo, Mexico. There were no land-based reports of sustained tropical-storm-force winds associated with Lorena. Tropical-storm-force gusts were reported across the southern portion of Baja California Sur, however, with a 53-kt wind gust measured in Cabo San Lucas and a 44-kt gust measured in Sierra La Laguna (Table 2).

trecho: Winds and Pressure Lorena’s estimated peak intensity of 75 kt from 1800 UTC 3 September to 0000 UTC 4 September is based on a blend of aircraft data and TAFB subjective Dvorak intensity estimates. The two reconnaissance missions by the AFRES into Lorena provided valuable data. The first mission sampled peak flight-level winds of 79 kt, 6 n mi to the northeast of the flight-level center at 1700 UTC 3 September. Using standard reduction factors from flight-level (700 mb), the surface winds were estimated to be around 71 kt. During this same mission, a dropsonde measured a 70-kt surface wind in the northeast eyewall. The WL150 and MBL winds from this dropsonde both suggested surface winds of 64 and 63 kt respectively. These data support a peak intensity of 75 kt when accounting for undersampling, and are further supported by the TAFB subjective Dvorak intensity estimates of T4.5/77 kt at 1800 UTC 3 September and 0000 UTC 4 September.

trecho: No fatalities or injuries can confidently be attributed to Lorena. There were several media reports indicating Lorena was responsible for several fatalities in the Mexican states of Nayarit and Sinaloa. However, after reviewing the articles and cross-referencing satellite imagery for the dates and times when the fatalities occurred, it was determined that these deaths were neither directly or indirectly related to Lorena. In Baja California Sur, impacts were concentrated in the municipalities of Los Cabos, La Paz, Mulegé, Loreto, and Comondú. Heavy rainfall and flooding resulted in water inundation of at least eight homes, while three additional residences were reported to have been swept away by floodwaters. Civil protection authorities reported approximately 50 vehicles stranded due to flooded or damaged roadways. Four landslides were also documented, and there was a minor disruption to electrical service associated with damage to a single power pole. Roadways across Los Cabos were engulfed in thick mud and debris due to the flooding, necessitating a substantial response and recovery effort. A total of 119 people sought refuge in four temporary shelters during the event. Numerous federal, state, and municipal agencies participated in preparedness and emergency response activities.

trecho: The genesis of Lorena was well anticipated. The tropical wave from which Lorena developed was first highlighted in the Tropical Weather Outlook (TWO) 156 h prior to formation (Table 3). The 7-day genesis probability was raised to the medium category 114 h before formation and to the high category 72 h in advance. Two-day genesis forecasts were also excellent. Low probabilities were introduced 78 h prior to formation, medium probabilities 48 h in advance, though high probabilities were introduced only 6 h before development occurred. Forecasts of Lorena’s genesis location were highly accurate, with the system forming within each of the genesis forecast areas depicted in NHC’s Graphical TWO, resulting in a 100% hit rate (Fig. 7). A verification of NHC official track forecasts for Lorena is given in Table 4a. Official track forecast errors were higher than the mean official errors for the previous 5-yr period at all forecast intervals. This is likely attributable to a bias in some of the model guidance keeping Lorena a deeper cyclone longer and steering the system into Baja California, while in actuality Lorena weakened much faster than anticipated and remained well offshore of Baja California steered by the low-level flow. A homogeneous comparison of the official track errors with selected guidance models is given in Table 4b.

trecho: Mario produced gusty winds and heavy rainfall when it passed just offshore of the coast of southwestern Mexico as a small tropical storm. After briefly degenerating into a trough, Mario redeveloped into a stronger tropical storm that moved over open waters well offshore of the Baja California peninsula. Tropical Storm Mario 11–16 September 2025

Mario appears to have originated from a tropical wave that crossed Central America and emerged over the eastern Pacific Ocean on 8–9 September. The wave produced disorganized showers and thunderstorms while moving westward, and a broad area of low pressure formed in association with the wave on 10 September, a couple of hundred n mi south of the coast of southern Mexico. The broad low turned northwestward while convective activity increased and gradually became better organized. Passive microwave data and satellite images indicate a well-defined, low-level circulation center formed early on 11 September, and it is estimated that a tropical depression formed by 0600 UTC that day, about 160 n mi southeast of Acapulco, Mexico. After briefly moving north-northwestward, the depression turned west-northwestward later on 11 September while moving around a low-to mid-level ridge over northern Mexico and Texas. The depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Mario by 0000 UTC 12 September, about 70 n mi southeast of Acapulco. The “best track” chart of Mario’s path is given in Fig. 1, with the wind and pressure histories shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively. The best track positions and intensities are listed in Table 11.

trecho: Satellite images, surface observations, and microwave data show that the circulation of Mario was very small on 12 September while the tropical storm passed near the southwestern coast of Mexico (Fig. 4). Convection became less organized later that day due to the negative effects of moderate northeasterly shear, dry air entrainment, and the storm’s close proximity to land. The small circulation became less defined and elongated in satellite images and scatterometer data, and Mario opened into a surface trough by 0000 UTC 13 September. Some deep convection flared up along the trough axis that morning while the remnants of Mario moved westward and interacted with a mesoscale convective system that moved off the coast of west-central Mexico. By midday, scatterometer data revealed the presence of a small but well-defined area of low pressure that formed in association with the remnants of Mario. This low moved west-southwestward to westward while being steered by a ridge to the north. The associated convection was disorganized late on 13 September, but increased in coverage and organization early the following morning. Mario became a tropical depression again by 0600 UTC 14 September, then strengthened into a tropical storm 6 h later when it was located about 270 n mi south of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.

trecho: As Mario passed near the coast of southern Mexico, the Acapulco International Airport (MMAA) reported a peak sustained wind of 22 kt and a gust of 32 kt at 0315 UTC 12 September. A couple of days later, an automated Mexican Navy weather station on Socorro Island recorded a peak wind gust of 29 kt at 1730 UTC 14 September and a minimum sea level pressure of 1001.6 mb just before 0000 UTC 15 September as Mario passed near the island. The following day, an inland weather station at Ciudad Constitución in Baja California Sur reported a sustained wind of 21 kt and a gust of 37 kt at 1610 UTC 15 September while Mario passed well offshore. Rainfall and Flooding Mario and its remnants contributed to an extended period of rainfall that occurred across portions of southwestern and west-central Mexico and the Baja California peninsula from 11–16 September (Fig. 6). The heaviest rainfall occurred on 12–13 September when Mario made its closest approach to the southwestern coast of Mexico, and a couple of stations in Guerrero and Colima reported more than 6 inches (~150 mm) of rainfall during the 24-h period. Media reports2 indicate some localized flooding occurred in parts of Guerrero, including Acapulco and Zihuatanejo.

Maximum reported Mexico rainfall totals by state from 11–16 September: Guerrero: 9.06 inches (230 mm) at Laguna de Coyuca, Coyuca de Benítez Nayarit: 8.58 inches (218 mm) at Gaviotas, Bahía de Banderas Colima: 7.06 inches (179.2 mm) at P. deriv. trecho: Genesis The first genesis of Mario was not forecast well in advance (Table 2a). The incipient wave was introduced in the Tropical Weather Outlook (TWO) only 72 h prior to formation, and it reached the medium and high categories 60 h and 54 h before genesis, respectively. The disturbance was introduced with a low chance of development in the 2-day TWO 60 h before genesis. The 2-day probabilities were raised to the medium and high categories 36 h and 12 h before formation, respectively. In general, the global models did not provide a very strong signal for genesis until only a few days before Mario formed. The second genesis of Mario was not anticipated (Table 2b). The remnants of Mario were introduced with a low chance of formation in the 7-day (2-day) TWO only 18 h (12 h) prior to genesis. The 2-day probabilities did not reach the medium or high category before genesis was determined to have occurred in post analysis. Forecaster confidence for genesis was low because there were multiple vorticity centers present (including the remnants of Mario) within a broader gyre well south of Baja California. From the available model guidance, it was unclear whether these features would consolidate or remain separate, weaker features embedded within the broader circulation.

Ultimately, the redevelopment that occurred was from the low-level vorticity associated with the remnants of Mario. The location of Mario’s initial genesis was accurately forecast (Fig. 7), with all of the formation areas capturing the region where Mario formed. The genesis areas for Mario’s redevelopment were also accurate (Fig. 8), albeit with limited lead time. Track A verification of NHC official track forecasts for Mario is given in Table 3a. Official track forecast errors were lower than the mean official errors for the previous 5-yr period at 12–24 h and 72 h, but greater than the 5-yr means at 36–60 h and 96 h. Note that the forecast sample size is relatively small and irregularly distributed. This is due to a couple of factors: (1) Mario had a fairly short existence as a tropical cyclone, and (2) Mario briefly dissipated and is shown as a disturbance or low for about a day in the final best track. Current NHC verification practice only includes forecasts if the system was classified in the final best track as a tropical cyclone at both the forecast’s initial time and at the projection’s valid time. A homogeneous comparison of the official track errors with selected guidance models is given in Table 3b.

trecho: Hurricane Octave took a rather unusual track across the eastern Pacific as the cyclone was highly influenced by two other tropical cyclones, Hurricane Priscilla and Tropical Storm Raymond (Fig. 1). After tracking steadily west-northwestward for several days, Octave made an abrupt U-turn on 5 October. The cyclone was steered eastward beginning that day by an approaching upper-level trough to the northwest along with the breakdown of a subtropical ridge to the east of the cyclone, caused by the large circulation of Hurricane Priscilla. Octave was then influenced by the circulations of both Priscilla and Raymond during the next several days, as it tracked generally eastward and eventually dissipated by 10 October. The “best track2” positions and intensities for Hurricane Octave are listed in Table 1. The best track chart of Octave’s path is given in Fig. 2, with the wind and pressure histories along with available observations3 shown in Figs. 3 and 4, respectively. There were no surface observations of winds of tropical storm force associated with Octave. Origin The origin of Octave can be traced to a convective complex that developed over the higher terrain of the far northern portion of South America on 16–17 September, fueled by an influx of deeper moisture feeding in off the tropical Atlantic from the east.

The 7-day genesis probability was raised to the medium category 42 h before formation and to the high category 30 h in advance. Two-day genesis forecasts were a little better; low probabilities were introduced 60 h prior to formation, medium probabilities 30 h prior, and high probabilities 18 h before development occurred. Octave’s genesis location was on the south side of all genesis formation regions. However, the system formed within each of the genesis forecast areas depicted in NHC’s Graphical TWO, resulting in a 100% hit rate (Fig. 6). A verification of NHC official track forecasts for Octave is given in Table 3a. Official track forecast errors were lower than the 5-year means at all forecast intervals. trecho: Priscilla developed from a monsoon trough that formed over the eastern Pacific around 30 September. Convection gradually increased over the subsequent days as a broad circulation drifted west-northwestward off the southern and southwestern Mexican coast. The surface low became better organized on the night of 3 October, with a sustained burst of deep convection within the broad inner core. Satellite wind observations later confirmed the development of a well-defined surface circulation, and a tropical depression formed at 1200 UTC 4 October about 260 n mi south-southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico. The “best track” chart of Priscilla’s path is given in Fig. 1, with the wind and pressure histories shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively. The best track positions and intensities are listed in Table 11. Priscilla became a tropical storm 6 h later on 4 October while slowly moving northwestward along the periphery of a weak mid-level ridge centered over Texas. The large tropical storm moved over warm sea-surface temperatures of around 29 to 30°C and through an environment with strong upper-level divergence. Despite its large size and moderate easterly vertical wind shear, Priscilla steadily strengthened through 5 October while turning north-northwestward and it became a hurricane at 0000 UTC 6 October while centered about 250 n mi south-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico.

trecho: During the next 24 h, the hurricane showed little change in strength while it moved north-northwestward parallel to the coast of Mexico. Microwave and surface wind satellite data then indicated that, while the outer wind field remained rather broad, the inner core began to contract and the maximum winds steadily increased. Priscilla reached a peak intensity of 100 kt at 1800 UTC 7 October while located a couple of hundred n mi south-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California Peninsula. After reaching its peak intensity, Priscilla began a steady weakening trend as environmental conditions became increasingly unfavorable. On 8 October, satellite imagery showed a marked degradation of the cyclone’s inner core, with diminishing deep convection, warming cloud tops, and a poorly defined eye, and the system rapidly weakened from a major hurricane to a tropical storm. This weakening was attributed to decreasing sea-surface temperatures, increasing southwesterly vertical wind shear and increasing intrusions of dry air. Priscilla continued northwestward and then northward around the periphery of the mid-level ridge off the coasts of mainland Mexico and Baja California Sur. 1 A digital record of the complete best track, including wind radii, can be found on line at ftp://ftp.nhc.noaa.gov/atcf.

trecho: Raymond originated from a broad area of low pressure that evolved within the eastern North Pacific monsoon trough located a few hundred n mi off the coast of southern Mexico by 1 October. This broad low meandered within the same general area for a few days, accompanied by disorganized and intermittent bursts of convection. Between 4 and 6 October, however, the disturbance became less identifiable in both satellite imagery and scatterometer data. The evolution was partially due to the influence of Hurricane Priscilla, located around 700 n mi to the west-northwest, whose large circulation and convective envelope likely played a role in disrupting this smaller-scale feature within the monsoon trough and suppressing much of its convection. As Priscilla lifted northward and steadily weakened, convection developed and expanded near the coast of southern Mexico by 8 October. Successive scatterometer passes afterward revealed the broad low gradually becoming better defined. Despite these improvements, persistent easterly vertical wind shear and the system’s proximity to land, and the possibility that the low-level circulation moved inland likely delayed the organization of deep convection and development of a well-defined center. By 9 October, however, convective organization began to improve, with banding features developing over the western and southern semicircles. An overnight OSCAT-3 pass revealed a well-defined low-level circulation near the coast of southwestern Mexico.

The cyclone strengthened into a 35-kt tropical storm 6 h later. The “best track” chart of Raymond’s path is given in Fig. 1, with the wind and pressure histories shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively. The best track positions and intensities are listed in Table 1. After genesis, Raymond moved steadily west-northwestward to northwestward at 10–15 kt along the southern periphery of a strong mid-level ridge over northern Mexico and the south-central United States. Very warm sea surface temperatures and strong upper-level divergence supported modest intensification despite persistent easterly vertical wind shear. Raymond reached its peak intensity of 50 kt from 0600–1200 UTC 10 October while paralleling the southwestern coast of Mexico. Raymond began to encounter an increasingly hostile environment after reaching peak intensity, characterized by strong easterly shear, drier mid-level air, and weakening outflow. These factors caused deep convection to become increasingly displaced from the low-level center, and by early on 11 October the cyclone’s convective pattern had become ragged.

trecho: Raymond continued moving quickly northwestward toward Baja California Sur, and any remaining deep convection dissipated during the early morning hours. Raymond became a post-tropical remnant low by 1800 UTC 11 October, when it was nearing the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula. The remnant low turned northward and then north-northeastward between 11–12 October in response to an amplifying mid-latitude trough over the southwestern United States. The system moved over the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula between 0000–0600 UTC 12 October and then briefly emerged over the southern Gulf of California. Raymond is estimated to have dissipated by 1800 UTC 12 October before reaching the coast of northwestern Mexico near Los Mochis. The remaining moisture was advected northward across northwestern Mexico and into portions of the southwestern United States.

trecho: The potential for Raymond’s development was recognized more than five days before formation, with confidence increasing as the disturbance began to organize near the coast of southwestern Mexico. Table 3 provides the number of hours before genesis when the first NHC Tropical Weather Outlook (TWO) forecast was issued in each likelihood category. For the 7-day outlook, a low (<40%) chance of development was first indicated 138 hours prior to genesis, and the probabilities were raised to the medium (40–60%) category 126 hours before formation. The 7-day probabilities were increased to the high (>60%) category 60 hours before formation. For the 2-day forecast period, the disturbance was given a low and medium chance of genesis 60 and 42 hours before formation, respectively, and the probabilities were increased to the high category 18 hours prior to genesis. Despite the presence of vertical shear, the disturbance’s proximity to land, and the influence of Hurricane Priscilla to the northwest, the forecasts for Raymond’s genesis location were accurate. The location of genesis occurred within nearly all of NHC’s graphical 7-day outlook areas, resulting in a 96% hit rate for all probabilistic categories (Fig. 5). These results indicate that, although the exact timing of genesis was somewhat uncertain due to the environmental challenges noted above, the spatial forecasts of where Raymond would form were consistently well-predicted.

trecho: The “best track2” positions and intensities for Tropical Storm Sonia are listed in Table 1. The “best track” chart of Sonia’s path is given in Fig. 1, with the wind and pressure histories along with available observations3 shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively. There were no ship reports of tropical-storm-force winds associated with Sonia. Origin Sonia originated from a tropical wave that moved across Central America on 16–17 October. The wave entered the eastern Pacific basin on 18 October and moved westward at about 10 kt over the next several days while producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. A surface trough became evident in scatterometer data on 22–23 October, and convection gradually organized along this feature while the low-level circulation became tighter and better defined. It is estimated that a tropical depression formed by 0600 UTC 24 October, about 615 n mi south-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula. Peak Intensity and Minimum Pressure Sonia’s peak intensity of 45 kt from 1200 UTC 25 October to 1200 UTC 26 October is supported by T3.0/45-kt Dvorak classifications from TAFB and a blend of UW-CIMSS SATCON, AiDT, and D-MINT estimates that peaked between 44–48 kt during this period.
